Lightning Roulette and Multiplier Numbers: How the Extra Payout Changes the House Edge

Published November 6, 2026 · 9 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Walk into the live-dealer lobby of almost any legal online casino and you'll find a roulette variant promising multiplier payouts of up to 500 times your bet on a lucky straight-up number. It's one of the most popular live-dealer formats to launch in the last several years, and it's easy to see why: a standard straight-up bet paying 35 to 1 is exciting enough, but a number struck by "lightning" that pays 500 to 1 is the kind of moment that gets clipped and shared. What the marketing doesn't spell out quite as loudly is how that bigger number gets funded — and once you see the mechanism, the math turns out to be more interesting than "better odds" or "worse odds." It's neither. It's a redistribution.

How the multiplier feature actually works

The base game underneath the multiplier feature is an ordinary single-zero roulette wheel — 37 pockets, numbers 1 through 36 plus a single green 0, the same layout covered in our roulette basics guide. Before each spin, a random number generator strikes somewhere between one and five numbers on the betting layout with a "lightning" multiplier, each assigned its own random value from a set list that typically ranges from 50x up to as high as 500x. The wheel then spins as normal. If the ball lands on a number that was struck and you had a straight-up bet riding on it, your bet pays out at that number's multiplier instead of a standard payout. If the ball lands on a struck number you didn't bet, nothing special happens for you. If it lands on an unstruck number, straight-up bets resolve at a different, smaller fixed payout than you'd see on a standard wheel — and that detail is the whole story.

The short version: only straight-up (single-number) bets are eligible for the multiplier feature at all. Every other bet type on the layout plays exactly like ordinary roulette, multiplier feature or not.

The trade-off: a smaller base payout funds the big one

A standard single-zero roulette wheel pays 35 to 1 on a straight-up bet. On the lightning-style variant, that same bet pays 29 to 1 when it hits a number that wasn't struck that round — six units less than the standard payout, on every single straight-up win, struck or not, win or lose. That reduction isn't a separate fee tacked onto your wager; it's simply a lower fixed payout built into the paytable for this specific bet type, in exchange for the chance that your number gets struck and pays dramatically more instead. There's no additional charge on outside bets, and there's no charge at all unless you're betting a single number.

It's worth sitting with how that trade actually plays out across many spins. Most of the time, your straight-up number isn't one of the handful struck that round, so most of your wins land at the reduced 29-to-1 rate rather than the standard 35-to-1 rate. Occasionally — and it is genuinely occasional, since only a few of the wheel's 37 numbers get struck on any given spin — your number both lands and was struck, and you collect a payout that dwarfs anything a standard wheel could offer on the same bet.

The math: why the long-run edge doesn't change

This is the part that surprises most players: despite the flashy multipliers, the long-run house edge on a straight-up bet in this format lands at roughly the same figure as a standard single-zero wheel, around 2.7%. The multipliers aren't free money layered on top of the game's existing payback — they're paid for entirely by the six units shaved off every non-struck straight-up win. Spread across enough spins, the extra money won on the rare struck-and-hit outcomes and the money given up on the much more common reduced-payout outcomes even out to almost exactly the same expected return a player would get from a plain 35-to-1 single-zero game.

Standard single-zero wheelLightning-style wheel
Straight-up payout, non-struck number35 to 129 to 1
Straight-up payout, struck numberN/A — no multiplier feature50 to 1 up to roughly 500 to 1 (randomly assigned)
Approximate house edge, straight-up bets~2.70%~2.70%
Approximate house edge, outside bets (red/black, odd/even, dozens)~2.70%~2.70% (unchanged, no multiplier eligibility)
Session-to-session variance on straight-up betsHigh (standard roulette variance)Much higher (occasional very large multiplier wins)

In other words: the house isn't giving away extra value by advertising a 500x number, and it isn't quietly padding its cut either. It's running close to the same game with the payout distribution reshaped — fewer, bigger wins instead of a steadier stream of standard-sized ones.

Outside bets: untouched by any of this

None of the reduced-payout mechanics apply outside of straight-up bets. Red or black, odd or even, high or low, columns, and dozens all pay exactly what they'd pay on a standard single-zero wheel, and none of them are eligible for a multiplier no matter how many numbers get struck that round. If you'd rather sidestep the whole trade-off entirely — the smaller standard payout, the long stretches without a multiplier hit — sticking to outside bets gets you the same house edge as the base straight-up game on a normal wheel, with none of the volatility swing. The feature genuinely only exists inside the straight-up betting area of the layout.

Same edge, very different variance

House edge tells you what a bet costs on average over a very long run. It says nothing about how bumpy the ride is getting there, which is the concept our slot volatility guide covers in more depth for a different game type — the same idea applies here. A standard single-zero straight-up bet is already one of the higher-variance bets on a roulette table, since it only wins once every 37 spins on average. Stacking a rare, huge multiplier on top of an already-infrequent outcome pushes that variance considerably higher still: most sessions betting straight numbers will see nothing but the reduced 29-to-1 payouts, if they see wins at all, while a small share of sessions will include one outsized hit that can completely change the shape of that session's results.

Takeaway: two players can both play this format with the same bet size and the same bet type for the same number of spins and walk away with wildly different results, purely from variance — one hitting a struck number for a few hundred times their bet, the other grinding through nothing but reduced-payout wins. That spread is normal for this format, not a sign anything is off.

Who this format actually suits

If the appeal of roulette for you is the occasional big number hitting — the kind of moment that makes a session memorable regardless of whether it's the mathematically optimal way to bet — this format delivers that in a way a standard wheel structurally can't. If you're playing for steadier, more predictable session outcomes, the reduced straight-up payout plus the added variance makes this a worse fit than a plain single-zero wheel, and sticking to outside bets (or a standard table entirely) will get you a calmer ride at the same long-run cost. Either way, the same bankroll principles apply as to any high-variance casino bet: size your stakes so a long cold stretch of reduced-payout, no-multiplier spins doesn't put a dent in money you need, and treat a big multiplier hit as a pleasant outlier rather than something to expect on a given session. Our casino bankroll management guide walks through sizing bets around exactly this kind of swing.

Frequently asked questions

Does the multiplier feature make Lightning-style roulette a better bet than standard roulette?

Not mathematically. The long-run house edge on straight-up bets works out to roughly the same figure as a standard single-zero wheel, since the big multiplier payouts are funded by a smaller fixed payout on every other straight-up win. What changes is the shape of the results, not the average outcome.

Can outside bets like red/black or odd/even ever get a multiplier?

No. The multiplier feature applies only to straight-up, single-number bets. Every other bet type pays its standard amount regardless of how many numbers are struck that round, and carries the same house edge as it would on an ordinary wheel.

How many numbers get struck with a multiplier each spin?

It varies by round — typically somewhere between one and five of the wheel's numbers are randomly struck before each spin, each assigned its own multiplier value. Most spins strike only a small handful out of the 37 possible numbers, which is why hitting a struck number with a straight-up bet is a relatively rare event.

Why does a non-struck straight-up win pay less than on a normal roulette table?

That reduced payout is how the format funds its multiplier feature. Rather than charging a separate fee, the game simply pays straight-up bets at a lower fixed rate on every non-struck win, and that difference is what makes the occasional much larger multiplier payout possible without changing the game's long-run edge.

Is this format riskier than standard roulette for the same bet size?

In terms of variance, yes — results swing more widely from session to session because wins are rarer but occasionally much larger. In terms of long-run expected loss, no — the house edge on both straight-up and outside bets is close to what you'd see on a standard single-zero wheel.
